'''''Hardenbergia violacea''''' is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Fabaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to Australia. It is known in Australia by the common names '''false sarsaparilla''', '''purple coral pea,''' and '''waraburra'''.<ref name="RBGS">{{NSW Flora Online|genus=Hardenbergia|species=violacea|author=C. Gardner}}</ref> Elsewhere it is also called '''purple twining-pea''', '''vine-lilac,''' and '''wild sarsaparilla'''.<ref>{{GRIN | accessdate = 12 January 2018}}</ref> It is a [[prostrate shrub|prostrate]] or climbing [[subshrub]] with egg-shaped to narrow lance-shaped leaves and [[raceme]]s of mostly purple flowers.
[[Image:Hardenbergia monophylla.jpg|thumb|Illustration by [[Edward Minchen]] in [[Joseph Maiden]]'s ''The Flowering Plants and Ferns of New South Wales'', as ''Hardenbergia monophylla''<ref name="Maiden">{{cite book |last1=Maiden |first1=Joseph |title=The Flowering Plants and Ferns of New South Wales |date=1896 |publisher=NSW Government Printing Office |location=Sydney |page=54 |url=https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=chi.14543598&view=1up&seq=112&q1=Hardenbergia |access-date=18 September 2021}}</ref>]]
[[File:Hardenbergia violacea HC1.JPG|thumb|Blossom detail]]

==Description==
''Hardenbergia violacea'' is a prostrate or climbing sub-shrub with wiry stems up to {{cvt|2|m}} or more long. The leaves are egg-shaped to lance-shaped, {{cvt|30–100|mm}} long and {{cvt|10–50|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] about {{cvt|10|mm}} long. The leaves are leathery, [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]] and paler on the lower surface.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Jeanes |first1=Jeff A. |title=''Hardenbergia violacea'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/b0aae4f9-9366-431a-b65d-7bd7de457797 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=18 September 2021}}</ref><ref name="efloraSA">{{cite web |title=''Hardenbergia violacea'' |url=http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/speciesfacts_display.cgi?form=speciesfacts&name=Hardenbergia_violacea |publisher=State Herbarium of South Australia |access-date=18 September 2021}}</ref><ref name="dpipwe">{{cite web |title=''Hardenbergia violacea'' |url=https://dpipwe.tas.gov.au/Documents/Hardenbergia-violacea-LS.pdf |publisher=Tasmanian Government Department of Primary Industries, Parks, Water and Environment |access-date=18 September 2021}}</ref><ref name="ANPSA">{{Cite web |url=https://anpsa.org.au/plant_profiles/hardenbergia-violacea/ |title=Australian Native Plants Society (Australia) (ANPSA): ''Hardenbergia violacea'' |access-date=18 September 2021 }}</ref><ref name="lucid">{{cite web |last1=Wood |first1=Betty |title=''Hardenbergia violacea'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/plants_se_nsw/text/entities/hardenbergia_violacea.htm |publisher=Lucid Keys |access-date=18 September 2021}}</ref>

The flowers are arranged in racemes of between twenty and forty flowers, each on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] mostly {{cvt|2–4|mm}} long. The [[sepal]]s are {{cvt|3–4|mm}} long and joined at the base, forming a bell-shaped tube with triangular teeth. The petals are about {{cvt|8|mm}} long, mostly purple, the [[Papilionaceous flower#Corolla|standard]] petal with a yellowish spot and a notch on the summit, the [[Papilionaceous flower#Corolla|wings]] are egg-shaped with the narrower end towards the base and the [[Papilionaceous flower#Corolla|keel]] is curved. Flowering mostly occurs from August to November and the fruit is a [[Pod (fruit)|pod]] {{cvt|20–45|mm}} long containing between six and eight kidney-shaped seeds. The flowers are usually purple or violet, but pink, white and other colours sometimes occur.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="efloraSA" /><ref name="dpipwe" /><ref name="ANPSA" /><ref name="lucid" />

''H. violacea'' regrows from its roots after [[Bushfires in Australia|fire]].<ref name=DPIpaddockplants>[http://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/agriculture/resources/private-forestry/paddock-plants/Hardenbergia-violacea-False-Sarsaparilla.pdf False (or Native) Sarsaparilla] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304121415/http://www.dpi.nsw.gov.au/agriculture/resources/private-forestry/paddock-plants/Hardenbergia-violacea-False-Sarsaparilla.pdf |date=2016-03-04 }}, Paddock Plants, NSW Department of Primary Industries (2010).</ref> The roots were experimented with by early European settlers as a substitute for [[Smilax regelii|sarsaparilla]].<ref name=DPIpaddockplants/>

==Taxonomy==
False sarsaparilla was first formally described in 1793 by [[George Voorhelm Schneevoogt]] who gave it the name ''Glycine violacea'' in his book, ''Icones Plantarum Rariorum''.<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Glycine violacea''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/521370 |publisher=APNI|access-date=18 September 2021}}</ref><ref name="Schneev.">{{cite book |last1=Schneevoogt |first1=George V. |title=Icones Plantarum Rariorum |date=1793 |page=29 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/132452#page/125/mode/1up |access-date=18 September 2021}}</ref> In 1940, [[William T. Stearn]] transferred the species to ''Hardenbergia'' as ''H. violacea'' in the ''[[Journal of Botany, British and Foreign]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Hardenbergia violacea''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/538251 |publisher=APNI|access-date=18 September 2021}}</ref><ref name="Stearn">{{cite journal |last1=Stearn |first1=William T. |title=Bibliographical Notes. Schneevoogt and Schwegman's Icones Plantarum Rariorum. |journal=Journal of Botany, British and Foreign |date=1940 |volume=78 |page=70 |url=https://archive.bsbi.org.uk/Journal_of_Botany_1940.pdf |access-date=29 November 2023}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Hardenbergia violacea'' grows in a variety of habitats but is more common in open forests, woodlands and undisturbed areas, from sea level to about {{cvt|1000|m}} above sea level. It occurs in eastern Queensland, eastern New South Wales, south-eastern Victoria and southern South Australia. There is a single population in Tasmania, where the species is listed as "endangered" under the Tasmanian Government ''[[Threatened Species Protection Act 1995]]''.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="efloraSA" /><ref name="dpipwe" />

==Use in horticulture==
''Hardenbergia violacea'' is widely grown as a garden plant, with many [[cultivar]]s now available.<ref name="ANPSA"/> It is hardy in mild and coastal areas of the United Kingdom where temperatures do not fall below {{convert| -5|C|F|abbr=on}}, but it does require a sheltered, south or west facing situation. Alternatively it may be grown indoors with full daylight, for instance in an unheated conservatory or greenhouse. It has been given the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Hardenbergia violacea''|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/8260/Hardenbergia-violacea/Details | accessdate=23 February 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 43 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 3 March 2018}}</ref>

The seeds of ''H. violacea'' remain viable for many years and propagation is from seeds that have been treated by adding boiling water to them or by abrading the seed coat. Plants prefer full sun in well-drained soil, are moderately frost-tolerant and respond well to pruning.<ref name="ANPSA" /><ref name="ABV">{{cite web |title=''Hardenbergia'' |date=24 September 2005 |url=https://www.abc.net.au/gardening/factsheets/hardenbergia/9426406 |publisher=Australian Broadcasting Corporation |access-date=18 September 2021}}</ref>
